task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-01, in the area of player absence and offensive reorganization):
How much the offense reorganizes (relative to L) predicts the change in points per possession.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=986; n=148, mde rho; 148 spells

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: predictive relationship between reorganization and PPP change
methodological_questions: How to measure offensive reorganization relative to a baseline L
Whether reorganization magnitude during absence spells predicts change in team points per possession
How to control for confounding by opponent defensive strength and simultaneous roster changes
Power and minimum detectable effect size given limited number of absence spells (n≈148)
Reliability of derived play-type possession metrics for short absence spells

historical_evidence.finding: Connector absence displaces team offensive identity (D_A) more than usage-matched non-organizer absence. Unmatched conn vs role D_A 0.2020 vs 0.1021, t=5.97 p=2.87e-08. Usage-matched vs role: paired dD_A +0.1151, P(conn>ctrl)=81.2%, t=6.35 p=7.35e-09 n=96. Vs terminal: +0.0777 t=2.37 p=0.0261 n=25.

A possession's ending state changes opponent points/possessions in the next 90-180s. 90s vs MADE_DEAD: TURNOVER_LIVE dOppPts=+0.510 dNetPts=-0.306 (dOppPPP=+0.055, dOppPoss=+0.298); MISSED_DEAD dNetPts=-0.112; PUTBACK dNetPts=+0.078. Volume, not PPP, carries most of the live-TO cost.
Putback suppression apparent effect on next possession vanishes after matching on game state; raw effect was a score/context confound.
Apparent next-game playing-time response to opponent 3P luck (G_opp3 +0.0625 SE 0.0180) disappears when controlling for game-N role (+0.0020 SE 0.0178), revealing a confound artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Causal isolation of putback suppression on next possession without adequate control for score/state confounds
failed_approaches.why: Confounding by game state (score, margin) produced a spurious effect that collapsed after matching; labeled artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attributing next-game playing-time changes to opponent 3P luck without controlling for the player's game-N role
failed_approaches.why: Confounding by game-N share; effect disappeared after including that control, establishing artifact.

evidence_establishes: Connector absences produce a larger break in offensive identity (D_A) than usage-matched non-organizer absences, confirming that absence type influences reorganization magnitude.
Prior artifact cases (SF-[prior work], [prior work]) demonstrate that apparent relationships in basketball data often vanish once confounds like game state or player role are properly controlled.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the amount of offensive reorganization predicts the change in points per possession; no prior study tested this predictive link.
The expected effect size or direction of any relationship between reorganization and PPP change.
The reliability and stability of the reorganization metric across different absence spell lengths and contexts.
own_inferences: The research question is novel in the context of this project's prior work: the predictive component has not been addressed.

The available data (n≈148 absence spells) and the inherent noisiness of both reorganization and PPP metrics likely yield low power, making a definitive test unlikely to produce a clear supported/rejected outcome.

Even if a statistical association were found, confounding by opponent defensive strength, simultaneous injuries, and schedule could produce spurious correlations, as seen in SF-[prior work] and [prior work].
Without a validated reorganization metric and careful handling of baseline (L) and measurement error, any test risks being an artifact.
A well-controlled regression with team/season fixed effects and opponent adjustments would be the minimum viable design, but it is still severely underpowered with current data.
uncertainties: The exact operational definition of L and the reorganization metric (how much the offense reorganizes relative to L) has not been specified or validated.
The possession count per absence spell and the resulting reliability of both reorganization and PPP change measures are unknown but likely low for short spells.
No prior estimate exists for the correlation between reorganization and PPP change, making power calculations speculative.
Spell selection criteria (minimum games, possessions) will further reduce the effective sample size below 148.
The partial 2025-26 data may introduce further noise or incomplete spells.

historical_effect.explanation: No prior decision existed. The historical evidence directly informed the assessment: [prior work][prior work] shows that reorganization can be measured and varies by absence type, while SF-[prior work] and [prior work] illustrate the serious risk of confounding artifacts. This reinforced the caution against proceeding without addressing low power and confounders, but did not change a pre-existing decision.

blocking_constraints.text: Only ~148 absence spells are available, many of short duration, yielding low power to detect a modest correlation between noisy measures. After requiring minimum possessions, effective sample size will shrink further.

The relationship between reorganization and PPP change is highly susceptible to confounding by opponent defensive strength, home/away, rest, and other roster changes; prior artifact cases (SF-[prior work], [prior work]) underscore this risk.

The reorganization metric derived from play-type distributions likely has low reliability for short spells, and PPP change is notoriously noisy; measurement error will attenuate any true signal and inflate required sample size.
Absences often follow extreme offensive performance; regression to the mean could create a spurious correlation between apparent reorganization and PPP change if not properly controlled.

prior_work.summary: [prior work][prior work] established that connector absences cause larger offensive identity breaks (reorganization) than usage-matched non-organizer absences, but did not test whether reorganization predicts changes in points per possession. No prior work has examined this predictive relationship.

risks.text: Insufficient number of absence spells (n≈148, reduced after quality filters) to reliably detect a plausible effect size against measurement noise.
Opponent strength, schedule, and simultaneous roster changes may drive both perceived reorganization and PPP changes, creating spurious associations.
Both the reorganization metric (derived from play-type distributions) and PPP change are measured with substantial error, especially for short absence spells.
Absences often follow extreme periods; without careful baseline adjustment, regression to the mean may masquerade as a reorganization-PPP relationship.
Many absence spells have too few possessions to estimate the reorganization metric reliably, forcing either exclusion or low-quality measurements.
If the baseline L uses information from the absence period or post-absence, the reorganization measure may be contaminated by outcomes.

design.estimand: Linear regression slope of the change in team offensive rating (points per 100 possessions) from the pre-absence baseline to the absence period on a continuous measure of offensive reorganization (e.g., divergence of play-type frequencies from the pre-absence L, computed over the first 5 games of the absence).
design.unit: Absence spell (a specific player's continuous missed games).
design.sample: All absence spells of at least 3 games and with at least 100 offensive possessions in both the pre-absence window (last 10 team games before absence) and the absence window, from the 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons.
design.power: For n=148 spells, power to detect a correlation of 0.20 is approximately 0.66 at α=0.05 two-sided; after correcting for measurement error, likely below 0.50. With additional future seasons (~250 spells) power could reach 0.80 for r=0.20.
design.controls: Team fixed effects, season fixed effects, opponent adjusted offensive rating (10-game rolling average), home/away indicator, days of rest, number of other missing rotation players, and pre-absence team offensive rating (to account for regression to the mean).
design.falsification: Test that the same reorganization measure does not predict change in team defensive rating (points allowed per 100 possessions). A null result on defense would support specificity.
design.multiplicity: Single primary hypothesis; no additional hypothesis tests beyond the falsification check, so no multiplicity adjustment required.
design.decision_rule: Reject null of zero slope if p < 0.05 (two-sided) with cluster-robust standard errors by team. Otherwise report the effect size with 95% confidence interval and declare the result inconclusive.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular season per-game play-by-play, substitution rotation, and derived play-type possession records, as of 2026-11-01.
